title: Incremental emission handshake and tool-call degradation acceptance spec
creator: Asha Patel
description: Purpose: Define acceptance criteria and tests for incremental JSON emission (partial objects), the runtime handshake required for invoking external tools/functions, and precise degradation modes when tool invocation fails or the stream ends mid-object.

Goal: Ensure product behavior is well-specified for engineering, QA, and client SDKs so that callers can reliably parse progressive outputs, detect tool-call boundaries, and implement safe fallbacks without data loss or inconsistent state.

Background: Multiple customer incidents revealed inconsistent behavior when streaming structured outputs containing nested objects and tool-call tokens. We need a deterministic spec describing streaming object boundaries, handshake signals, idempotency expectations, and well-defined error/fallback policies.

Scope: This ticket covers acceptance criteria, example traces, error modes, and test cases for the hosted API and SDKs. It excludes cloud-provider networking retries, Dedicated capacity scheduling, and on-prem upgrade mechanics.
Out of scope: SDK UI/UX for displaying partial objects, billing changes, internal kernel scheduling optimizations.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Handshake header: Every streaming response that may invoke a tool MUST include a top-level handshake event within the first 256 bytes: "tool_handshake:v1". SDKs and parsers should use this to enable structured parsing mode.

2) Partial-object framing: When emitting partial JSON objects the stream MUST emit a marker event before the first fragment of a top-level object and after the final fragment. Markers are simple tokens: "__OBJ_START__" and "__OBJ_END__" emitted as separate stream frames. Parsers must reconstruct object text by concatenating fragments between markers.

3) Tool-call envelope: A tool invocation MUST be represented as a top-level object with keys {"tool_call":true, "tool_name":string, "call_id":uuid, "args":object}. The call_id is required and MUST be globally unique per request. When streamed, args may be emitted incrementally inside the object framing rules.

4) Idempotency and retries: If the same call_id is delivered multiple times due to retries or reconnection, runtimes and tools MUST treat duplicate call_id as idempotent: only the first successful invocation should be executed. The model/client is responsible for re-sending the same call_id if it retries.

5) Mid-object cutoff semantics: If the stream ends before a matching __OBJ_END__ is observed, the runtime MUST emit a final error frame with code "incomplete_object" and include the last observed call_id (if any). The client may choose to abort or attempt a best-effort reconcile using the partial object contents.

6) Error propagation and fallback: If tool invocation fails (tool returns a 5xx or times out), the system MUST emit a structured failure event referencing call_id and a recommended fallback action: "retry", "fallback_response", or "skip_tool". The model may be invoked to continue using the provided fallback action with a deterministic indicator in the stream.

7) Backpressure behavior: If downstream tool invocation is slower than the model's generation, the serving runtime MUST apply controlled backpressure: it can either buffer up to 1MB of in-flight fragments per request or throttle model token emission. The chosen behavior must be consistent per-model-config and reported via the API response headers at connection start.

8) Observability hooks: Each tool-handshake, start/end of object, tool invocation result, and incomplete_object error MUST be emitted to the console tracing stream and logged with request_id and call_id for later debugging and correlation.

9) Schema versioning: The handshake token supports a version (e.g., tool_handshake:v1). Newer versions must be backwards compatible or negotiated via an optional "schema_versions" capability list in the handshake frame. SDKs must allow unknown future fields without failing.

10) Streaming security: For private deployments, the handshake MUST include a token hash header to attest that the customer-managed KMS signed the request if KMS is enabled. Failure to validate should result in an immediate connection close with reason "kms_validation_failed".

11) Test coverage: Automated end-to-end tests covering normal full-object streams, incremental-args streams, duplicate call_id retries, mid-stream cutoffs, tool slowdowns/backpressure, and tool 5xx responses must pass in CI before marking Done.

12) Client SDK behavior: Official JS/Python SDKs must expose a high-level helper that reassembles partial objects, surfaces error codes (incomplete_object, tool_error, kms_validation_failed), and supplies an easy callback for idempotent retries using call_id.
13) Rollout policy: The feature must be behind a runtime feature-flag by default; 10% host traffic for the canary rollout, increasing to 100% after 2 weeks and no high-severity issues are reported.

14) Backwards compatibility: Existing non-handshake streaming responses must continue to be processed by the SDKs in legacy mode; new handshake frames are optional for models that do not emit tool calls.
15) Documentation: Public API docs and console UX guides updated with protocol examples, sample trace logs, and migration notes for SDK consumers.
implementation_notes: Prefer a minimal binary-safe framing for handshake/markers to avoid ambiguity with user-generated text (we use simple ASCII tokens in first release).
Server: Add handshake injection logic in streaming head writer and ensure header is within initial frame budget.
Runtime: Implement per-request buffering + token emission throttle and expose config controls at model bundle level.
Tools: Add call_id dedup table with TTL = 24h to ensure idempotent behavior across retries.
SDKs: Provide reassembly utilities that operate on stream frames and emit reassembled JSON objects or well-defined error events.
test_plan: Unit tests for framing parser with fragmented object streams (start/mid/end across frames).
Integration test that simulates tool 5xx and verifies fallback event emitted and SDK behavior matches acceptance criteria.
Chaos test: abrupt connection close mid-object to validate incomplete_object emission and downstream client handling.
Load test to validate backpressure strategy under heavy concurrent tool invocations (target 95th pct latency < 500ms for tool handoff under baseline).
E2E canary tests in staged environment with 10% traffic toggle exercising schema negotiation and handshake presence.
risks_mitigation: Risk: Clients may embed the ASCII tokens in generated text, causing false framing. Mitigation: choose tokens unlikely to occur in normal text and document the tokens in SDKs; plan to move to length-prefixed frames if collisions occur.
Risk: Tool dedup table state explosion. Mitigation: TTL and shard boundaries, and fall back to best-effort dedup when table capacity is saturated (emit metric & trace).
Risk: Increased latency due to backpressure. Mitigation: provide per-model config to prefer buffering vs throttling and monitor unit economics impact via console metrics.
acceptance_examples: Example 1 - normal flow: handshake frame -> __OBJ_START__ -> {"tool_call":true,"tool_name":"search","call_id":"uuid-123","args":{"q":"foo"}} fragments -> __OBJ_END__ -> tool result frame -> model continuation frame.
Example 2 - mid-stream cutoff: handshake -> __OBJ_START__ -> partial args fragments -> connection close -> server emits error frame {"error":"incomplete_object","call_id":"uuid-123"}.

Example 3 - tool failure: full call object -> runtime invokes tool -> tool 504 -> runtime emits {"call_id":"uuid-456","status":"tool_error","recommended_action":"fallback_response"} and model receives fallback token to continue.
